The repository identifies LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models as a paper describing LoRA [1](#source-1).

According to the repository, LoRA adapts pretrained language models by learning pairs of low-rank adaptation matrices while freezing the original weights [1](#source-1).

The repository for LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models reports that LoRA reduces the number of trainable parameters [1](#source-1).

The repository for LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models reports that LoRA reduces storage requirements for large language models adapted to specific tasks [1](#source-1).

## Method and implementation

The repository for LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models states that LoRA can be applied to any subset of pretrained weights [1](#source-1).

The repository for LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models suggests exploring adaptation of multilayer perceptron layers [1](#source-1).

The repository considers it very likely that the optimal LoRA configuration varies across model architectures and tasks [1](#source-1).

The repository identifies loralib as a Python package [1](#source-1).

## Capabilities and deployment

The documented loralib workflow marks only LoRA parameters as trainable before the training loop [1](#source-1).

The documented loralib workflow saves a checkpoint containing only LoRA parameters rather than the entire model state [1](#source-1).

The repository for LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models states that using its LoRA checkpoints still requires the original pretrained checkpoint from Hugging Face [1](#source-1).

The repository for LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models documents loading the pretrained checkpoint before the LoRA checkpoint with strict=False for both loads [1](#source-1).

The repository reports that LoRA reduces storage requirements for large language models adapted to specific tasks [1](#source-1).

The repository reports that LoRA enables efficient task switching during deployment [1](#source-1).

The repository documents that calling model.eval() in loralib merges LoRA parameters with the corresponding pretrained weights unless merge_weights=False is passed to the LoRA layers [1](#source-1).

The repository reports that merging LoRA parameters with pretrained weights through model.eval() in loralib eliminates additional latency for subsequent forward passes [1](#source-1).

The repository for LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models documents that calling model.train() again reverses the evaluation-mode weight merge [1](#source-1).

The repository for LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models documents disabling automatic weight merging by passing merge_weights=False to LoRA layers [1](#source-1).

The repository documents optional bias training alongside LoRA in loralib by passing all or lora_only to the bias argument of mark_only_lora_as_trainable [1](#source-1).

The authors state that the LoRA paper did not thoroughly study the effects of training bias vectors alongside LoRA [1](#source-1).

The repository reports evaluating LoRA on GLUE using RoBERTa base and large and DeBERTa XXL against fine-tuning baseline numbers taken from Liu and colleagues in 2019 and He and colleagues in 2020 [1](#source-1).

The repository for LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models reports 4700000 trainable parameters for DeBERTa XXL with LoRA [1](#source-1).

The repository for LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models lists 1500000000 trainable parameters for the DeBERTa XXL full-fine-tuning baseline [1](#source-1).

The repository for LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models reports evaluating LoRA on E2E NLG Challenge using GPT-2 in comparisons with full fine-tuning, adapters, and prefix tuning [1](#source-1).

The repository for LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models reports evaluating LoRA on DART using GPT-2 in comparisons with full fine-tuning, adapters, and prefix tuning [1](#source-1).

The repository for LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models reports evaluating LoRA on WebNLG using GPT-2 in comparisons with full fine-tuning, adapters, and prefix tuning [1](#source-1).

## Related work

The QLoRA paper describes QLoRA as an efficient fine-tuning approach that reduces memory usage [3](#source-3).

The authors describe QLoRA as backpropagating gradients through a frozen, four-bit quantized pretrained language model into LoRA adapters [3](#source-3).

The authors describe four-bit NormalFloat as information-theoretically optimal for normally distributed weights [3](#source-3).

The QLoRA paper describes a lemon-picked analysis of where Guanaco fails compared with ChatGPT [3](#source-3).

review.originalMarkdown:
LoRA, short for Low-Rank Adaptation, is a method for adapting pretrained language models by freezing their original weights and learning pairs of rank-decomposition matrices instead [1](#source-1). This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the storage needed for task-specific adaptations [1](#source-1). The paper introducing the method is credited to Edward J. Hu, Yelong Shen, Phillip Wallis, Zeyuan Allen-Zhu, Yuanzhi Li, Shean Wang, Lu Wang, and Weizhu Chen, and is listed in the project repository as an International Conference on Learning Representations 2022 publication [1](#source-1).

## Method and implementation

LoRA represents trainable adaptations using pairs of low-rank matrices while leaving the corresponding pretrained weights unchanged during training [1](#source-1). The authors’ implementation examples primarily adapt the query and value projections in Transformer models, although the repository states that LoRA can be applied to other subsets of pretrained weights, including embeddings and multilayer perceptron layers [1](#source-1). The repository also notes that the best configuration may vary across model architectures and tasks [1](#source-1).

The official implementation, the Python package `loralib`, supports PyTorch and provides adapted versions of linear, embedding, and two-dimensional convolution layers [1](#source-1). It also provides a `MergedLinear` layer for implementations that combine multiple projections, such as attention query, key, and value projections, into one linear layer [1](#source-1). A February 2023 repository update announced support for LoRA in Hugging Face’s Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning library [1](#source-1).

## Storage and deployment

The documented training workflow marks LoRA parameters as trainable and saves a checkpoint containing those parameters rather than the entire model [1](#source-1). Such a checkpoint still requires the original pretrained checkpoint: the documented loading procedure loads the pretrained model first and then the LoRA parameters [1](#source-1). The authors describe the reduced storage requirement as enabling efficient switching between task-specific adaptations during deployment [1](#source-1).

According to the repository documentation, entering evaluation mode in `loralib` merges LoRA parameters with the corresponding pretrained weights, eliminating additional latency from the adaptation in subsequent forward passes [1](#source-1). Returning to training mode reverses that merge, and automatic merging can also be disabled [1](#source-1). The implementation optionally allows bias vectors to be trained alongside LoRA parameters, although the authors state that they did not thoroughly study this option in the paper [1](#source-1).

## Reported performance and comparisons

The authors’ repository reports results comparable or superior to full fine-tuning on the GLUE benchmark using RoBERTa and DeBERTa, with substantially fewer trainable parameters [1](#source-1). For RoBERTa base, its table lists 0.8 million trainable parameters for LoRA versus 125 million for full fine-tuning, with reported average scores of 87.24 and 86.40, respectively [1](#source-1). For DeBERTa XXL, the corresponding figures are 4.7 million versus 1.5 billion trainable parameters and average scores of 91.32 versus 91.06 [1](#source-1).

The repository also reports GPT-2 evaluations on E2E, DART, and WebNLG, comparing LoRA with full fine-tuning, adapters, and prefix tuning [1](#source-1). These comparisons combine the authors’ experiments with baseline results drawn from earlier papers, as identified in the repository [1](#source-1).

A research preprint by Reece Shuttleworth and colleagues, first submitted in October 2024 and revised in October 2025, questions whether LoRA and full fine-tuning learn equivalent solutions [2](#source-2). Its authors report that LoRA produces new, high-ranking singular vectors in model weight matrices, termed intruder dimensions, that are absent from their full-fine-tuning comparisons [2](#source-2). They find that LoRA forgets less overall in their study, but that its forgetting is strongly localized to these dimensions and that their accumulation accompanies worse performance in the continual-learning setting examined [2](#source-2).

## Quantized adaptation with QLoRA

QLoRA extends low-rank adaptation by backpropagating gradients through a frozen, four-bit quantized pretrained language model into LoRA adapters [3](#source-3). Its authors report fine-tuning a 65-billion-parameter model on a single 48 GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit fine-tuning task performance [3](#source-3). Its memory-saving techniques include four-bit NormalFloat, double quantization of quantization constants, and paged optimizers for managing memory spikes [3](#source-3).

The QLoRA study reports experiments involving more than 1,000 models across eight instruction datasets, including LLaMA and T5 models, alongside human and GPT-4 evaluations [3](#source-3). The authors also caution that contemporary chatbot benchmarks were not trustworthy measures of chatbot performance and present an analysis of failures of their Guanaco models relative to ChatGPT [3](#source-3).
